title: Definition of Ready and Definition of Done
blurb: Tell the Definition of Ready from the Definition of Done, apply 'done or not done', and know where each is set.
question: At the end of an iteration, a team says a story is '90% done' and asks to count it. Separately, it wants a rule that stops vague stories entering the iteration. Which agreement covers each situation?

teach.body: The Definition of Ready (DoR) is a shared team agreement on the criteria an item must meet before work begins: clear objectives, clearly defined scope, and the information, resources and dependencies in place. The Definition of Done (DoD) is a shared agreement on the criteria an item must meet to be considered complete, such as review, validation and approval. One guards the start; the other guards the finish.

teach.h: DoR and DoD side by side
Done or not done: there is no 'almost'
teach.body: Under the DoD, an item is either done or not done; agile has no 'almost done'. If only part of a story is finished, split it: the finished part, if it meets the DoD, counts as done, and the rest goes back to the backlog to be reprioritized. Work that still has defects is not done. This keeps progress honest, because burn charts and velocity count only finished work.

root.label: Story at the end of the iteration

teach.body: Both definitions are quality practice artifacts. In the team planning workshop, the user story refinement topic checks that acceptance criteria are clear and testable and clarifies what counts as done. During delivery, the tester reviews products against the acceptance criteria and the team DoD. At project level, the project DoR and DoD are agreed as topics of the project initiation workshop.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.2; Tables 13.7, 13.13; Table B.1

teach.body: Product owner Kwame Mensah's team is building a repairs portal. The story 'report a leak with a photo and choose an appointment' meets the DoR: who, what and why are written, acceptance criteria are agreed and access to the photo store is confirmed. At the iteration's end, tester Lucy Barton finds the photo upload meets the DoD but slot booking is unfinished. The team splits the story: the upload counts as done and booking returns to the backlog.

teach.text: DoR is about STARTING; DoD is about FINISHING. 'All acceptance criteria met, reviewed and approved' is DoD territory, not DoR. And a story at 90% is not done: split it or leave it out of the count.

items: DoR: criteria an item must meet before work begins (9.3.2.1).
DoD: criteria an item must meet to be considered complete (9.3.2.2).
Done or not done; no 'almost done'. Split partly done stories.
Work with defects is not done.
Project DoR and DoD: agreed in the project initiation workshop, shown in the project backlog.
Team DoD: included in or linked from the product backlog; the tester checks against it.

summary: You can now tell the Definition of Ready from the Definition of Done and apply the 'done or not done' rule to a partly finished story. You can also say where the project and team versions are set.

A.q: What is the Definition of Ready?
options: Criteria an item must meet before work on it begins
Criteria an item must meet to be considered complete
The list of stories selected for the next iteration
The board's approval to start the next stage
A.why: The DoR is a shared team agreement on the criteria an item must meet before work begins (9.3.2.1).

whyNot.1: Criteria for being complete are the Definition of Done.
whyNot.2: Selecting stories for the iteration is iteration planning, which produces the team plan.
whyNot.3: Stage authorization is a board decision in directing a project, not the DoR.

A.q: What is the Definition of Done?
options: The criteria an item must meet before work begins
Agreed criteria an item must meet to be complete
The date by which an iteration must finish
The approval the board gives at project closure
A.why: The DoD is a shared agreement on the criteria an item must meet to be considered complete (9.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Criteria to start work are the Definition of Ready.
whyNot.2: The iteration end date comes from the timebox, not the DoD.
whyNot.3: Board approval at closure is the 'authorize project closure' activity.

A.q: A tester finds that a story works but still has two known defects at the end of the iteration. How should it be treated?
options: As done, with the defects recorded
As almost done, to finish next time
As ready for the next release
As not done under the DoD
A.why: Work with defects is not done, and agile has no 'almost done' (9.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Logging the defects does not make the story done; it fails the DoD.
whyNot.1: There is no 'almost done' category in agile.
whyNot.2: Ready relates to starting work; a defective story is not ready for release.

B.q: Which would MOST likely appear in a Definition of Ready for a user story?
options: It has passed every test and been approved by users
It has been demonstrated in the progress review
It has who, what, why and acceptance criteria
It has been released to live users in production
B.why: A story is ready when it contains who, what and why and has measurable, prioritized acceptance criteria (9.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: Passing tests and approval are completion criteria, part of the DoD.
whyNot.1: A demonstration happens after the work is built, not before it starts.
whyNot.3: Release to users happens after work is done, not before it begins.

B.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. The DoR helps prevent delays by making sure the team has what it needs to start.
2. The DoD allows a story to be recorded as almost done.
3. A partly done story is split, with the unfinished part returned to the backlog.
4. The DoR is checked when a story is claimed complete.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: The DoR prevents delays and misunderstandings (1), and a partly done story is split with the rest returned to the backlog (3) (9.3.2.1, 9.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: there is no 'almost done'.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: there is no 'almost done', and the DoR is checked before work begins.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: completion is checked against the DoD, not the DoR.

B.q: In which workshop are the project Definition of Ready and project Definition of Done agreed?
options: Project initiation workshop
Project canvas workshop
Release planning workshop
Project kickoff workshop
B.why: The project DoR and project DoD are topics of the project initiation workshop (Table 13.7).

whyNot.1: The project canvas workshop builds the canvas (users, options, vision, benefits, risks, scope, costs, value).
whyNot.2: The release planning workshop, at a stage boundary, covers OKRs and updating the release map.
whyNot.3: The kickoff workshop covers team values, skill and delegation matrices and dashboards.

C.q: Where is the team Definition of Done included or linked, and who owns that artifact?
options: Project backlog; chief product owner
Release map; project manager
Team dashboard; team coach
Product backlog; product owner
C.why: The product backlog includes or links to the team DoD, and the product owner owns it (8.3.2.1, Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The project backlog shows the project DoR and DoD, not the team DoD.
whyNot.1: The release map is the project and stage plan; it does not hold the DoD.
whyNot.2: The team dashboard shows team progress; the team coach does not own an artifact holding the DoD.

C.q: At the end of an iteration, a story has two of its three acceptance criteria met. What does PRINCE2 Agile suggest?
options: Record it as done and fix the gap in the next release
Extend the iteration until the last criterion is met
Split it and return the unfinished part to the backlog
Mark it as two-thirds done on the team dashboard
C.why: A partly done story is split: the finished part counts if it meets the DoD, and the rest returns to the backlog for reprioritization (9.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: It is not done while a criterion is unmet, so it cannot be recorded as done.
whyNot.1: The timebox is fixed; iterations are not extended to finish items.
whyNot.3: There is no partial or 'almost done' status in agile.

C.q: Which role reviews products against the acceptance criteria and the team Definition of Done?
options: Developer
Tester
Project assurance
Team coach
C.why: The tester designs and runs tests and reviews products against acceptance or quality criteria and the team DoD (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The developer designs, builds and maintains increments of the product.
whyNot.2: Project assurance monitors adherence to principles, practices and governance, not each product against the DoD.
whyNot.3: The team coach helps the team self-manage and facilitates workshops.

reteach.title: Boarding gate and arrivals gate
reteach.question: Think of a flight: one check before you board and one when you land. How does that map onto the DoR and DoD?

blocks.body: Before boarding you need a ticket, a passport and your bag checked in: that is the Definition of Ready, everything needed to start. On landing you have arrived or you have not; nobody is 'almost in Madrid'. That is the Definition of Done: the item meets every agreed criterion or it is not complete.

blocks.text: If the question is about STARTING work, think DoR. If it is about COUNTING work as complete, think DoD.

explain.body: A shared team agreement on what an item needs before work starts: clear objectives and scope, plus the information, resources and dependencies in place. It helps prevent delays and misunderstandings.

test.q: What does a Definition of Ready MAINLY help prevent?
options: Unplanned scope changes to the project backlog
Defects reaching live users after release
Delays and misunderstandings once work starts
Costs running over the agreed stage budget
test.why: The DoR makes sure the team has everything it needs to start, which helps prevent delays and misunderstandings (9.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: Changes to the agreed project scope are controlled through the issues practice; the DoR governs when an item can start.
whyNot.1: Stopping defects reaching users is the job of the DoD and testing.
whyNot.3: Cost has zero tolerance and is controlled through plans and progress, not the DoR.

explain.body: A shared agreement on the criteria for an item to be complete. Something is done or not done; work with defects is not done.

test.q: Which statement reflects the Definition of Done?
options: An item can be 80% done at review
An item is either done or not done
An item is done once coding stops
An item is done when its iteration ends
test.why: Under the DoD, something is either done or not done; there is no 'almost done' (9.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Partial percentages are exactly what 'no almost done' rules out.
whyNot.2: Finishing coding is not enough; review, validation and approval may still be needed.
whyNot.3: The end of the timebox does not make unfinished work done.

explain.body: The project DoR and project DoD are agreed in the project initiation workshop and shown in or linked from the project backlog. The team DoD is included in or linked from each product backlog.

test.q: The project Definition of Done sets criteria for work to be acceptable to whom?
options: The senior supplier and the developers
The project manager and project support
The agile coach and the team coach
The users and the chief product owner
test.why: The project DoD sets the criteria for work to be acceptable to the users and the CPO (Table 13.7).

whyNot.0: The supplier side builds the product; the project DoD is about user acceptance.
whyNot.1: The PM and project support manage and administer; they are not the acceptors.
whyNot.2: Coaches support agile ways of working; they do not accept the product.

explain.body: Rules about whether an item may START (clear scope, dependencies resolved) belong to the DoR. Rules about whether it is FINISHED (tested, approved, no defects) belong to the DoD.

test.q: A team agrees that a story may enter an iteration once its dependencies are resolved. Which agreement is this part of?
options: Definition of Ready
Definition of Done
Acceptance criteria
Quality register
test.why: Having dependencies in place before work begins is a Definition of Ready criterion (9.3.2.1).

whyNot.1: The DoD concerns when work is complete, not when it may start.
whyNot.2: Acceptance criteria describe what the story must do to be accepted.
whyNot.3: The quality register records planned and completed quality activities.
